paras: The hanging of contractor McKee was an assault in which railroad workers who said they had not been paid hanged McKee, a member of the Memphis contracting firm McTigh & Co., until he lost consciousness at Van Buren, given as Arkansas, around the end of February 1888. The men cut him down and revived him, and he survived. Wire reports told it as the opening of a chain of violence in Shannon county, Missouri, that included a killing and two lynchings.

McTigh & Co. of Memphis held the contract for the Current River branch of the Gulf Railroad, which had been extended to the village of Winona, and sublet the work to sub-contractors including George Madden. According to a Springfield, Missouri, dispatch, the day-laborers had gone unpaid for some time, and the sub-contractors calmed them by saying they too had received nothing from the firm, which turned the men's anger toward 'the unknown moneyed men.'

On a Wednesday, McKee arrived at Van Buren to look over the work and was met by men demanding their money. He refused to pay until he had seen the construction engineer's estimate, and the men dragged him, from his carriage in one version, to the court house yard. There they put a rope around his neck and, after he fought back, hung him up until his face blackened and his body went limp.

The two versions of the dispatch differ on what followed. The New York Sun's version said the rope was cut, whiskey was poured into him, and the frightened McKee 'got the money and paid the men.' The version printed in the Sacramento Record-Union said the men threw water in his face and let him go, and that he drove off to take a train out of the country.

After the hanging, sub-contractor Madden demanded money from McKee, a fight followed in which Constable John Rucker intervened, and Rucker later shot Madden dead. Railroad hands then hunted Rucker, and two of his friends were reported lynched. No arrest or prosecution for the hanging of McKee appears in the coverage.

The hanging reached distant papers only through Springfield wire dispatches, printed by The Sun in New York on March 6 and the Sacramento Daily Record-Union on March 7. The Sun headed its story 'Several Victims of the Row' and remarked that the men 'wanted money, not a life,' while the Record-Union headed it 'Sanguinary Affair' with the subhead 'A Capitalist Strung Up.' A separate St. Louis dispatch, run on March 6 by the St. Paul Daily Globe and the Waco Daily Examiner, focused on Madden's death, named McKee only as the superintendent Madden had threatened to shoot, and did not mention a hanging.

Besides the outcome, the dispatches differ on who hanged McKee: the Sun says 'a dozen sub-contractors,' the Record-Union the laborers whom the bosses could no longer control. The place is also uncertain, since the dispatches label it Van Buren, Arkansas, yet the Record-Union has McKee drive from the hanging to Van Buren to catch a train, in a story otherwise set around Winona, Missouri.

reader.title: Hanging of contractor McKee by unpaid railroad workers
bases: Workers on a railroad branch who said they were unpaid hanged a member of the contracting firm until he was unconscious to force payment of their wages (A1, A6).

McKee survived: he was cut down or lowered and revived (A1, A6). The dozen or more men acted without legal authority, but to extort unpaid wages, not under a pretext of justice; A1 says they 'wanted money, not a life.'

The hanging appears only in two versions of a Springfield, Mo., wire dispatch (A1, A6) that agree on the core event; the separate St. Louis dispatch on the same railroad trouble (A2, A3) names McKee but does not mention a hanging.

accounts.label: Springfield wire, March 5
accounts.gist: A dozen sub-contractors met McKee at Van Buren, hanged him in the Court House yard until limp, cut him down and revived him with whiskey; frightened, he got the money and paid them.

accounts.label: Springfield wire, March 6
accounts.gist: Unpaid day-laborers dragged McKee from his carriage, hanged him until insensible, revived him with water and let him go; he drove off to catch a train out of the country.

accounts.label: St. Louis wire, March 5
accounts.gist: Madden, pressed by his laborers for pay, threatened to shoot McKee on Saturday morning; no hanging of McKee is mentioned.

framing.detail: The Sun ran it under 'Several Victims of the Row' as part of 'Miscellaneous Shooting' in Missouri, stating the men 'wanted money, not a life.'
The Record-Union headed it 'Sanguinary Affair' with the subhead 'A Capitalist Strung Up,' describing the laborers' anger turning on 'the unknown moneyed men.'
